t2−t−2=(t−2)(t+1)=0.

Join the centre of the unit circle to adjacent vertices of the regular polygon. Each of the n resulting triangles has two sides of length 1 and included angle 2π/n. Bisecting one gives a right triangle, so each polygon side, a chord of a circle, has length 2sin(π/n). Thus the perimeter is 2nsin(π/n).
Each of these triangles has area 21​sin(2π/n), so the polygon's area is 2n​sin(2π/n). Comparing the two expressions gives
m=2,k=2.​

The removed vector is the orthogonal projection of r onto the line through the origin in direction n^. The remaining vector measures the perpendicular displacement from that line. Fixing its Euclidean norm at 2 therefore describes an infinite circular cylinder of radius 2, with axis x=z, y=0.

The plane equation x+z=0 has normal vector (1,0,1)T=2​n^. Thus its normal vector is parallel to the cylinder's axis and the plane is perpendicular to that axis. It passes through the origin, so the intersection is a circle of radius 2 centred at the origin in that plane.
Indeed, with the orthonormal basis e=(1,0,−1)T/2​ and f=(0,1,0)T of the plane, write r=se+tf. The cylinder equation becomes s2+t2=4. Equivalently, the intersection has the parametric equation
r(θ)=2cosθe+2sinθf,0≤θ<2π.​
(23)

Let d=a2​−a1​ and w=v1​×v2​. The assumed linear independence gives w=0. Every displacement joining one line to the other is
s=d+λ2​v2​−λ1​v1​.
(25)
Its dot product with w is always d⋅w. The component in that direction is therefore fixed, so orthogonal decomposition gives ∥s∥≥∣d⋅w∣/∥w∥.
The two linearly independent vectors v1​,v2​ span the plane perpendicular to w. Suitable λ1​,λ2​ cancel the component of d in that plane, attaining the lower bound. Thus the distance between skew lines formula, also valid when the lines intersect, gives
d(L1​,L2​)=∥v1​×v2​∥∣(a2​−a1​)⋅(v1​×v2​)∣​.​

The nonzero direction vectors now have linear dependence, so the lines are parallel or coincident. Subtract from d=a2​−a1​ its orthogonal projection along v1​; the remaining component is the shortest joining displacement. The distance between parallel lines is
d(L1​,L2​)=​d−v1​⋅v1​d⋅v1​​v1​​=∥v1​∥∥d×v1​∥​.​

The second expression follows from the relation between the cross product and the perpendicular component. It includes distance zero for coincident lines.

For the stipulated linearly independent vectors v1​,v2​, the denominator in part (i) is nonzero. Thus
d(L1​,L2​)=0⟺(a2​−a1​)⋅(v1​×v2​)=0.​

Equivalently, a2​−a1​ belongs to the linear span of v1​,v2​. Geometrically the lines lie in one plane, and, since their direction vectors are not parallel, they intersect at a unique point. The linear combination expressing a2​−a1​ gives the two parameters of that intersection.

Dividing these power series gives the hyperbolic tangent expansion
tanhx=(x+6x3​+O(x5))(1−2x2​+O(x4))=x−3x3​+O(x5)​.

Multiply the two power series, retaining every contribution through degree four:

The stated parameter restrictions ensure that the logarithm is defined near x=1, and that F′(1)>0 and F′′(1)<0. With h=x−1, the Taylor series begins
F(1+h)=ln(ea−b)+ea−baea​h−2(ea−b)2a2bea​h2+O(h3).

If ea−b=1, the constant term is nonzero, and the first two nonzero terms are

This covers both a>ln(1+b) and 0<a<ln(1+b); the constant term is respectively positive or negative.

Where cosx=0, the separable differential equation is y′=ytanx. Separating and taking antiderivatives gives ln∣y∣=−ln∣cosx∣+C, for nonzero y. Including the zero solution, the explicit general solution is
y(x)=Csecx,C∈R,​
(55)
on any interval with cosx=0. It can also be obtained without dividing by y: the product rule gives (ycosx)′=0.
A nonzero solution cannot extend through a zero of cosx. If a differentiable solution is required on an interval containing such a zero, the original equation there requires y=0, and the only such solution across that zero is y≡0.

Taking antiderivatives yields v2=2ln∣x∣+C. The explicit general solution is therefore

Replacing y2 by u suggests the potential

Direct differentiation verifies that dH/dx is exactly the left-hand side of the required ordinary differential equation. This direct verification remains valid even for negative u; it does not require a real square root y=u​. Therefore

The initial condition gives C=1. Solving this quadratic equation in u and selecting the branch that has u(1)=0 gives
u(x)=2x2−1+1+4x2−4x4​​=1+1+4x2−4x4​2(1−x2)​.​

The second expression also defines the removable value u(0)=1. The maximal open interval containing 1 on which this is a differentiable real solution is

At either endpoint the square root vanishes and 2x2u+1=0, while x(u2+1)=0, so the original ordinary differential equation cannot hold there with a finite derivative.

Solution

c OurBigBook.com
In the translated coordinates u=x−1, v=y+1, the zero level set is the pair of lines u=0 and v=0. The function is positive in the quadrants uv>0 and negative in those with uv<0, and tends to zero as u2+v2→∞. Thus its nonzero contours form closed curves around the four off-centre stationary points.
For an explicit description of the contour plot, use polar coordinates u=rcosθ, v=rsinθ:
f=2r2​e−r2/2sin2θ.
(67)
At fixed direction within a quadrant, the magnitude increases until r=2​ and then decreases towards zero. Also ∣u∣e−u2/2≤e−1/2, with equality exactly when ∣u∣=1, and similarly for v. Consequently ∣f∣≤e−1; each positive level below e−1 encloses a positive peak in each positive quadrant, with the analogous negative contours in the negative quadrants.
To classify the stationary points, the Hessian matrix is
∇2f=E(uv(u2−3)(1−u2)(1−v2)​(1−u2)(1−v2)uv(v2−3)​).
(68)
At u=v=0 it is (01​10​), with eigenvalues 1 and −1, so (1,−1) is a saddle point. At u,v∈{−1,1} it is −2fI. Therefore (2,0) and (0,−2) are strict local maxima, and (2,−2) and (0,0) are strict local minima. These are also global maxima and minima by the bound just proved.

The gradient is
∇f=E(v(1−u2),u(1−v2))T.​
(69)
It is perpendicular to each nonzero level set and points towards increasing f. Near the two positive local maxima, the Hessian matrix is −2e−1I, so the gradient arrows point inward. Near the two negative local minima, the Hessian matrix is 2e−1I, so they point outward. These arrows are shown on the figure in part (c).
At the saddle point, ∇f≈(v,u)T. Along v=u, the arrows point away from the centre on both sides; along v=−u, they point towards the centre on both sides. On the positive u axis they point up, on the negative u axis down, on the positive v axis right, and on the negative v axis left. This specifies the four intervening sectors of the gradient pattern.

A Fourier series represents a periodic function as a constant plus sine and cosine waves whose frequencies are integer multiples of its fundamental frequency. For period 2L, use the convention
f(x)∼2a0​​+∑n=1∞​[an​cos(Lnπx​)+bn​sin(Lnπx​)],
(84)
where the Fourier coefficients are
a0​an​bn​​=L1​∫−LL​f(x)dx,=L1​∫−LL​f(x)cos(Lnπx​)dx,n≥1,=L1​∫−LL​f(x)sin(Lnπx​)dx,n≥1.​​
(85)
The coefficient formulas follow by multiplying by a basis sine or cosine and using their orthogonality over a full period. A Fourier series need not equal an arbitrary function at every point. The pointwise convergence of a piecewise smooth Fourier series theorem says that for a piecewise continuously differentiable function, the Fourier series converges at each point to the average of the two one-sided limits, and hence to f(x) wherever f is continuous.

Let G=x2/a2+y2/a2+z2/b2−1. Its gradient cannot vanish on the ellipsoid, since the origin is not on the surface. Thus the Lagrange multiplier equations capture every constrained stationary point:
4x3=a22λx​,2yz2=a22λy​,2y2z=b22λz​,a2x2+y2​+b2z2​=1.​
(107)
The temperature is a sum of squares, so T≥0. Equality requires x=0 and yz=0. The surface constraint then gives the four coldest points:
Tmin​=0,(x,y,z)=(0,±a,0) or (0,0,±b).​
(108)
These are all such points, because a sum of nonnegative terms can vanish only when each term vanishes.

b

Solution

b OurBigBook.com
Solve the Lagrange multiplier equations by separating cases according to which coordinates vanish, so that division by a coordinate loses no stationary points.
If x=0 and y=z=0, the surface constraint gives
(x,y,z)=(±a,0,0),T=a4.​
(109)
If x=0 and exactly one of y,z is nonzero, the equation for that nonzero coordinate forces λ=0, while the x equation gives λ=2a2x2>0. Hence there are no stationary points in that case.
If x=0 and y,z=0, the two remaining equations give λ=a2z2=b2y2. The surface constraint therefore has equal contributions from y and z, giving four stationary points:
(x,y,z)=(0,ε2​a​,η2​b​),T=4a2b2​,ε,η∈{−1,1}.​
(110)
If all three coordinates are nonzero, the equations imply
λ=2a2x2=a2z2=b2y2,
(111)
so z2=2x2 and y2=2a2x2/b2. Substitution in the surface constraint gives, with D=4a2+b2,
x2=Da2b2​,y2=D2a4​,z2=D2a2b2​.
(112)
Thus the remaining eight stationary points and their temperatures are
(x,y,z)=(ε1​D​ab​,ε2​D​2​a2​,ε3​D​2​ab​),T=4a2+b2a4b2​,ε1​,ε2​,ε3​∈{−1,1}.​
(113)
For example, their common temperature follows from x4+y2z2=a4b4/D2+4a6b2/D2=a4b2/D. The cases with x=0 and yz=0 are exactly the coldest points already listed. This exhausts all possibilities, giving fourteen other stationary points in addition to those four.

Tmax​=1,(x,y,z)=(1,0,0) or (−1,0,0).​
(114)
For a direct bound, put s=x2∈[0,1]. The identity (y2−z2)2≥0 gives y2z2≤(y2+z2)2/4=(1−s)2/4, and
T≤s2+4(1−s)2​≤1,
(115)
since 1−s2−(1−s)2/4=(1−s)(5s+3)/4≥0. Equality forces s=1, giving exactly the two points above.
